What the listing is made of is not obvious from the class names: the tools are GROUPED by program group with a heading and a summary per group, both the groups and the tools inside them are sorted, every line is coloured in escapes that are bytes like any other, a summary is TRUNCATED to the width the renderer chose so the golden holds what was printed rather than what the annotation says, and a beta or experimental tool carries a marker inside the line. The same text goes to stdout for no arguments and to stderr for a name that does not resolve, and both are recorded so a port that built one of them cannot pass.

cases.why: Two runs, four streams: the listing on stdout with the other stream empty, and the listing on stderr with stdout empty.

suites.title: whether two sequence dictionaries may be used together, and what the refusal says
suites.why: Four rows of CountVariants' covering array disagreed on this and nothing else: they pass a BAM to --input alongside a VCF to --variant, and GATKTool validates the two dictionaries against each other BEFORE the traversal, where the port counted (#1038). The outcome is one of eight named cases and the rules behind them are not guessable: a length of ZERO is equivalent to any length; reversing the common contigs is a SUPERSET without the ordering check and OUT_OF_ORDER with it, so an argument decides whether the same pair is accepted; the same relative order at different absolute positions is DIFFERENT_INDICES, a case of its own; a common subset is accepted unless a superset was required, and the refusal then names the MISSING contigs; and the human-order check needs chr1, chr2 and chr10 by name AND by length, firing on whichever dictionary is lexicographic.

cases.why: Fourteen pairs, each compared under both settings of the ordering flag and validated under all four combinations of the two flags.

suites.title: the five arguments that turn -L and -XL into the list a walker traverses
suites.why: The runners read --intervals and ignore the other four, so --interval-padding, --interval-exclusion-padding, --interval-set-rule and --exclude-intervals change nothing in the port and change the answer in the reference: four of the five arguments of the collection every walker carries. The rules are not guessable. Padding is applied PER -L argument, before the set operator, and each padded batch is sorted and merged with ALL whatever the merging rule is. The set operator folds one argument at a time into an accumulator, and an EMPTY accumulator short-circuits it, which is why the first -L is never intersected with anything and why INTERSECTION over three arguments is not the intersection of all three at once. An empty intersection is a REFUSAL rather than an empty traversal, and so is an exclusion that removes everything. -XL with no -L means the whole reference contig by contig. And `unmapped` is a traversal flag rather than an interval, accepted on -L and refused on -XL.

cases.why: Twenty-four command lines over one three-contig dictionary whose order is not alphabetical, covering each argument alone, the pairs that interact, and the three refusals.

suites.title: which read filters a command line actually ends up with
suites.why: The runner reads --read-filter and --disable-tool-default-read-filters and ignores the other two arguments the descriptor owns: --disable-read-filter and --inverted-read-filter change nothing in the port and change the filters, and therefore the count, in the reference (#69). The resolution is order-dependent and its rules are not guessable: disabling removes from the DEFAULTS only and before anything is added; an enabled filter already among the defaults is not added twice, and the check is contains() on INSTANCES rather than on names; an inverted filter is always added, as a negated instance, so inverting a tool default leaves both in the list; and the refusal for a filter that is both enabled and inverted prints the WRONG variable, so its message lists the empty set. That last one is the reference's behaviour and a port has to reproduce it.

cases.why: Seventeen command lines over one tool's three default filters, covering each argument alone, the pairs that interact, and the five refusals.

suites.title: the command line a tool records in every file it writes
suites.why: A BAM's @PG carries it in CL and a VCF's ##GATKCommandLine carries it in CommandLine, so it is a byte of the output for every record-transform and variant-transform tool there is: `sam_output::Options` takes it as an INPUT because no port could invent it, which is what stops PrintReads from having a runner (#69). The rule is not guessable from the string. It opens with the tool CLASS's simple name; the arguments come in two groups, those the user SET in the parser's declaration order and then those that were not set but have a non-null default, in that same order rather than the order they were typed; every one is printed as `--longName value` whatever the user typed, so a short alias is expanded and an `=` is separated; a collection becomes one pair PER ELEMENT; and a default of null is omitted where any other default is printed, which is why the line is long for a command line that set two arguments.

cases.why: Seven command lines over PrintReads covering each rule, and one over each of the other four declared tools so the opening name and the defaults behind it are measured rather than assumed to follow one pattern.

suites.title: handleNonUserException, which is the handler handleUserException is not
suites.why: `main-entry` measured `handleUserException` and left the other handler alone, so the port has one banner and prints it for both: a CountReads covering-array row shows the reference answering `java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Dictionary cannot have size zero` and the port answering `A USER ERROR has occurred: Dictionary cannot have size zero`, with the right message, the right status and the wrong wrapper (#1020). What the reference prints on this path is `printStackTrace` and nothing else: no banner, no prefix, no property notice, and a first line that is `Throwable.toString()`, which is the class's BINARY name, so a nested class prints with a `$`.

cases.why: Eight throwables: the two a read walker reaches, a null message and an empty one, a nested class of this harness and a nested class of the reference's own, a message that spans lines, and the Error overload. The frames are not committed -- they name this harness and its line numbers -- so each case carries its first line and whether everything after it was a frame.

suites.title: which stream each entry path writes to, what it returns, and the exit status an exception carries
suites.why: `mainEntry` ends in System.exit, so the mapping from an exception to a status is measured as the pair it is: the five constants read off the class, and the exception each path throws. What that pins is that a name which does not resolve exits 2 while a name which does but is given nothing exits 1, and that a Picard tool's non-zero return exits 4 through a wrapper the GATK side never sees.

cases.why: Thirteen cases: no arguments, `-h`, `--help`, a tool followed by `-h`, three spellings of the version, an unknown name, a deprecated one, a GATK tool and a Picard tool each given nothing, the two handlers on their own, and the version printed to a stream that is not System.out.

suites.title: the .sbi of a BAM, and the naming, granularity and refusals around htsjdk's writer
suites.why: The granularity counts RECORDS and not bytes, and the last field of the index is the offset the next record would have been written at, taken from the last record's chunk end rather than from the file's length. An empty BAM has no last record to ask, so that field falls back to the file length, and the two answers are different numbers.

cases.why: Fourteen cases: four granularities including the default and one above the record count, the default output name, the .bai companion, a queryname-sorted file with and without it, an empty BAM on both paths, a granularity of zero and of minus one, and a file that is not a BAM.

suites.title: the chi-squared statistic over the allele frequency bins, and the p-value it gives
suites.why: The statistic is not Pearson's: the expected count in the denominator is replaced by a constant variance, SQUARED, so raising --allowed-variance from a hundredth to a tenth divides the statistic by a hundred rather than by ten. The comparison set has to be given TWICE, once as --comp and once as a second eval track, or every bin holds a single row and the sum is nought whatever the data says. The bin ladder is fixed at sixty-one, so the degrees of freedom are sixty in every run and a bin no variant reached contributes a term of nought.

cases.why: Nine cases: het calls against the comparison frequencies, one bin called homozygous, two other variances, a threshold above the p-value, a filtered variant, a comparison site the call set has nothing at, a file with one variant in it, and a VCF with no alias header.

suites.title: the coverage filter, the table the genotyping is done from, and the two files
suites.why: The two ratio arguments are accepted and ignored: both fields are `private final double` initialised from a constant expression, which makes their one read a compile-time constant, so a low ratio of ten that would drop every site changes nothing. The filter itself still cuts at three times the mean, which the golden shows by keeping the same six homozygous-alternate sites at a lower depth and watching the answer move. And a matched normal decides WHICH sites are homozygous while the tumour's own counts are read there: 0.915 against 0.044 on the same tumour table.

cases.why: Eleven cases: a plain run, one asking for the segmentation, a table with sites under the minimum coverage, a deep hom-alt tail the ceiling cuts and the same tail at a depth it keeps, four ratio settings including one that would drop every site, a matched normal whose hom-alt sites sit elsewhere, one with no hom-alt site at all, and a matched normal with the segmentation.

suites.title: what one tool declares, and therefore which command lines it accepts
suites.why: The parser is measured mechanism by mechanism; what no suite holds is what any ONE tool declares. A read walker declares a handful of arguments of its own and ends up with dozens, the rest inherited from the collections its superclasses hold, in an order that is the parser's and not the source's. That flattened namespace is what Milestone C's per-tool declarations have to reproduce, and a variant walker having no `--input` at all is the cheapest proof that it cannot be guessed from the archetype. The declarations now carry the type, the primitiveness, the three visibility flags, the bounds, the mutex targets, the controlling plugin and the documentation, which is what a parser and a usage text can be BUILT from rather than only counted against.

cases.why: Re-measured with `CheckPileup` and `AnnotateIntervals` among the twenty-one declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `CompareIntervalLists` and `FixMisencodedBaseQualityReads` among the nineteen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `PrintDistantMates` and `GetSampleName` among the seventeen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `Pileup` and `PreprocessIntervals` among the fifteen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `CountBasesInReference` and `SplitIntervals` among the declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `CountBases` and `FlagStat` among the declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, as the candidate artefact of run 33713985893; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured without the sort, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, as the candidate artefact of run 33704325792; the mutex target list now carries the order it holds, which is the order the refusal joins it in (#1069). Seven tools' full declaration lists, and eighteen command lines over them: the empty one, the input alone under each spelling, the input twice, an unknown argument, one and two intervals, a variant argument given to a read walker and an input given to a variant walker, a print tool with and without its output and with its output twice, and a tool that is no walker at all.

suites.title: the usage text Barclay renders, which is a rendering and not prose
suites.why: The usage is generated from the same annotations the argument definitions come from, so it has an ordering, a grouping, a wrapping and a set of colour codes, and it is byte-comparable like anything else. Three tools of three shapes: a read walker whose usage carries the plugin arguments, and two tools that are no walkers and carry none.

cases.why: Re-measured with `CompareIntervalLists`, which is UNDOCUMENTED: the inventory carries a summary only for a documented tool, so this golden is where the declarations generator reads it. Three tools' whole usage text, its line count, and whether -h and --help agree.

suites.title: the BWA index image a reference produces, and where it lands
suites.why: The image is NOT byte-comparable: building one reference twice in a single process gives two files of the same length whose differing bytes are in-process POINTERS. The golden therefore holds the size, the landing name, the refusal and the fact of that instability, and says why the bytes are not a claim.

cases.why: Ten cases: one reference indexed twice, the same bases in lower case, a longer sequence, two contigs, a renamed contig, a run of Ns, a reference of one base, the default output name, and a fasta that is not there. Every case is built twice, and the golden records that no two builds agree.

suites.title: the constants an enum-valued argument accepts, and what a value outside them costs
suites.why: The declarations golden says an argument's type is IntervalSetRule and cannot say what one is. A parser needs the constants twice: to convert a value at all, and to write the message a bad one produces, which lists every constant in declaration order.

cases.why: Re-measured with `CheckPileup` and `AnnotateIntervals` among the twenty-one declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with the nineteen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `PrintDistantMates` and `GetSampleName` among the seventeen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with `Pileup` and `PreprocessIntervals` among the fifteen declared tools, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. Re-measured with the thirteen declared tools rather than the seven this dump was written with, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner; identical to the local smoke run. `IntervalListScatterMode` arrives with `SplitIntervals`, and an enum missing from this table is an argument the port's parser DROPS. One table of enum types with their constants in declaration order, the ClpEnum documentation where there is any, every enum-valued argument of the seven tools with its default, and seven command lines: two constants, a lower-case one, a value the type does not carry, an empty one, and the same pair on a second type.

suites.title: the four value classes a tool declares and the port cannot yet convert
suites.why: Every one of the seven ported tools declares a GATKPath, so no command line reaches the ported parser until these four conversions are measured. What a class accepts is what its String constructor accepts, which is why a File refuses nothing and a Float refuses what Float.valueOf refuses, naming Float where a Double's message names Double.

cases.why: Twenty-two command lines over one target carrying a field of each class: a path, a URI, a relative path, one that names nothing and an empty one; the same strings through a File; a tag on the taggable class, on the one that is not, and by short name; an empty and a filled collection; a FeatureInput tagged and not; and a Float on both sides of what Float.valueOf accepts, primitive and boxed.

suites.title: which read filter owns which controlled argument, and which of them are required
suites.why: The plugin trim drops a controlled argument whose plugin nobody selected, which is why a required argument of an unselected read filter does not fire on a plain command line. `barclay-plugin-descriptors` measured that rule; the table it runs over is a property of GATK's filter library and cannot be derived from the declarations golden, which records the descriptor and not the class that contributed the argument.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite, and identical to the local smoke run. 62 rows: 28 controlled arguments with their owning filter class, 12 of them required, then the six answers of isDependentArgumentAllowed with and without tool defaults and ten command lines through the trim.

suites.title: the read filter library, and which of them each tool takes as defaults
suites.why: A tool's DEFAULT read filters count as selected, so their arguments are accepted with no --read-filter on the command line, and the list is per tool rather than per descriptor. It is also what --disable-read-filter prints as its possible values and --read-filter prints the whole catalogue, so a walker's usage cannot be composed without both sets. Neither is derivable: the declarations record an argument's type as String and carry no possible values, and a filter with no arguments is in the catalogue and in no ownership row.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite, and identical to the local smoke run. The catalogue of 56 filters, then the nine declared tools: five walkers whose descriptor is `readFilter` and whose defaults are `WellformedReadFilter`, and four with no descriptor at all.

suites.title: the long name and the field name of a mutex target, which are not the same string
suites.why: `tool-argument-declarations` measured `getMutexTargetList()`, which is the long name a mutex target resolves to. The usage prints the FIELD name the annotation was written with, so `--ambig-filter-bases` reports `ambig-filter-frac` in one and `maxAmbiguousBaseFraction` in the other. Only one of the two was measured, which is why a walker's composed usage differs from the `usage-text` golden in exactly four lines.

cases.why: Re-measured without the sort, in the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, as the candidate artefact of run 33704325792; the mutex target list now carries the order it holds, which is the order the refusal joins it in (#1069). From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite, and identical to the local smoke run. Four mutex arguments, all of them a read filter's, over two of the four tools: the target's long name, the target definition's FIELD name, and the sentence the usage renders from the second.

suites.title: what CountReads returns and what it writes, which is the layer between the count and a command line
suites.why: `count-reads-and-bases` measures the number. What decides whether a port can RUN the tool is the layer around it: the value handleResult prints, the bytes -O receives (the number with no trailing newline, written with print rather than println), and the refusal a missing input earns before any of it.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite, and identical to the local smoke run. Nine command lines: the value the tool returns, the bytes the output file holds, and the two refusals.

suites.title: what a read walker does with a file that is not a BAM
suites.why: CountReads' covering array reproduces four of eighteen rows, and eleven of the fifteen it does not are one shape: a file the corpus carries for another tool handed to a read walker. The reference refuses those, and the refusal is neither the port's message nor the port's status: htsjdk reads a VCF as a SAM stream, finds no sequence dictionary and throws an IllegalArgumentException, which `Main` reports as a non-user failure.

cases.why: From the pinned container on a real x86-64 runner, published as the golden-pending artefact of the run that added this suite, and identical to the local smoke run. Eleven inputs and three kinds of refusal, plus the two that are not refused at all.
